parts.title: Part 1: A new neighbor
parts.intro: Mia sees a new person on her street.
paragraphs: Mia is a young woman. She lives in a small flat on Green Street. The street is quiet and there is a big tree in front of her window. She works in a bookshop, and she likes her job.
Today is Saturday. Mia is at home. She hears a loud noise outside. A big truck is in front of the house next door.
A man gets out of the truck. He is tall and he has short black hair. A small brown dog is with him. The dog has a red ball in its mouth.
"Hello!" says Mia. "Are you my new neighbor?"
"Yes, I am," says the man. "My name is Leo. This is my dog, Max."
"Nice to meet you, Leo," says Mia. "Can I help you?"
"Yes, please! I have many boxes," says Leo. He smiles.

parts.title: Part 2: Where is Max?

paragraphs: It is Sunday morning. Mia is in her kitchen. She has a cup of tea and a piece of bread. Suddenly, someone knocks on the door.
It is Leo. He looks very sad and tired.
"Mia, please help me!" he says. "Max is not at home. I can't find him!"
"Oh no!" says Mia. "Is the back door open?"
"Yes, it is," says Leo. "I think Max is outside. He has no collar, and he doesn't know this street."
Mia puts her cup on the table. "Don't worry," she says. "There is a park near here. Dogs like parks. Let's look there."
Mia takes her coat and her phone. Leo takes Max's red ball. "Max loves this ball," he says. "Maybe he can smell it."
They walk down Green Street together.

parts.intro: Mother Rabbit warns her four children not to go into Mr. McGregor's garden, but one of them does not obey.
paragraphs: Once upon a time there were four little Rabbits, and their names were—
Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter.
They lived with their Mother in a sand-bank, underneath the root of a very big fir-tree.

'Now my dears,' said old Mrs. Rabbit one morning, 'you may go into the fields or down the lane, but don't go into Mr. McGregor's garden: your Father had an accident there; he was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor.'
'Now run along, and don't get into mischief. I am going out.'
Then old Mrs. Rabbit took a basket and her umbrella, and went through the wood to the baker's. She bought a loaf of brown bread and five currant buns.
Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail, who were good little bunnies, went down the lane to gather blackberries:
But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor's garden, and squeezed under the gate!
First he ate some lettuces and some French beans; and then he ate some radishes;
And then, feeling rather sick, he went to look for some parsley.

parts.title: Part 2: Peter in the garden

paragraphs: But round the end of a cucumber frame, whom should he meet but Mr. McGregor!

Peter was most dreadfully frightened; he rushed all over the garden, for he had forgotten the way back to the gate.
He lost one of his shoes among the cabbages, and the other shoe amongst the potatoes.

After losing them, he ran on four legs and went faster, so that I think he might have got away altogether if he had not unfortunately run into a gooseberry net, and got caught by the large buttons on his jacket. It was a blue jacket with brass buttons, quite new.
Peter gave himself up for lost, and shed big tears; but his sobs were overheard by some friendly sparrows, who flew to him in great excitement, and implored him to exert himself.
Mr. McGregor came up with a sieve, which he intended to pop upon the top of Peter; but Peter wriggled out just in time, leaving his jacket behind him.

parts.title: Part 3: Lost among the plants
parts.intro: Peter hides, sneezes and escapes through a window, but he still cannot find the way out.
paragraphs: Mr. McGregor was quite sure that Peter was somewhere in the tool-shed, perhaps hidden underneath a flower-pot. He began to turn them over carefully, looking under each.
Presently Peter sneezed—'Kertyschoo!' Mr. McGregor was after him in no time.
And tried to put his foot upon Peter, who jumped out of a window, upsetting three plants. The window was too small for Mr. McGregor, and he was tired of running after Peter. He went back to his work.
Peter sat down to rest; he was out of breath and trembling with fright, and he had not the least idea which way to go. Also he was very damp with sitting in that can.
After a time he began to wander about, going lippity—lippity—not very fast, and looking all round.
He found a door in a wall; but it was locked, and there was no room for a fat little rabbit to squeeze underneath.

An old mouse was running in and out over the stone doorstep, carrying peas and beans to her family in the wood. Peter asked her the way to the gate, but she had such a large pea in her mouth that she could not answer. She only shook her head at him. Peter began to cry.

parts.intro: Peter finally sees the door, escapes from the garden and gets home very tired.

His back was turned towards Peter, and beyond him was the gate!
Peter got down very quietly off the wheelbarrow; and started running as fast as he could go, along a straight walk behind some black-currant bushes.
Mr. McGregor caught sight of him at the corner, but Peter did not care. He slipped underneath the gate, and was safe at last in the wood outside the garden.
Mr. McGregor hung up the little jacket and the shoes for a scare-crow to frighten the blackbirds.

I am sorry to say that Peter was not very well during the evening.

parts.title: Part 1: The wrong suitcase
parts.intro: Lena arrives in a small town by the sea for a short holiday.
paragraphs: Lena got off the train in Marbella Bay at four o'clock. The town was small and quiet, and the sea was bluer than in her photos. She was very happy. She had a week of holiday, and she was going to swim, read and do nothing.
At the station, a lot of people were waiting for their bags. Lena saw her suitcase at once. It was blue, and it had a yellow ribbon on the handle. She took it and walked to the hotel.

The Hotel Mar was old but friendly. Mr. Costa, the owner, gave her the key to Room 12. "Breakfast is at eight," he said. "The room is on the second floor. You can take the stairs, because the lift is broken."

parts.title: Part 1: A New Start
parts.intro: Elena leaves her old job and arrives in a small town to open a shop that is not quite empty.
paragraphs: Elena Ruiz had worked in a bank in Mexico City for eleven years when she finally decided to change her life. She was tired of numbers, meetings and the long journey to the office every morning. "If I stay here, I will never do anything different," she told her sister.

Three months later, she was standing in front of a small shop in a quiet town on the English coast. Her uncle Tomas, who had repaired clocks there for forty years, had moved to live with his daughter in Canada. Before he left, he had offered Elena the shop. "It isn't much," he had said on the phone, "but it's yours if you want it."

Elena had never repaired a clock in her life. However, she had always enjoyed fixing small things, and she had been learning from videos for weeks. If the shop failed, she thought, she could always go home. But she was determined to try.

Inside, the shop smelled of dust and oil. There were clocks everywhere: on the walls, on the shelves and even on the floor. While she was looking around, a man with a white apron knocked on the window. He was holding a paper bag.
"You must be Tomas's niece," he said with a smile. "I'm Mr Hale. I run the bakery next door. I've brought you some bread, because nobody should start a new job hungry."

Elena thanked him and asked how long he had known her uncle. "Thirty years," he answered. "He was a good neighbour. He told me you were coming, but he didn't say why he was in such a hurry to leave." He stopped for a moment. "Be careful, my dear. Last week, a man was asking questions about this shop."
"What kind of questions?" Elena asked.
"He wanted to know when you would arrive, and whether the shop was for sale," said Mr Hale. "I told him I didn't know anything."

That night, Elena slept in the small room above the shop. At about midnight, she woke up because she heard a noise downstairs. She took a torch and went down slowly. Nobody was there, but the door of the old oak cabinet was open, and one clock lay on the floor.

Later, she phoned her uncle. "Did anyone want something from the shop?" she asked. There was a long silence. Then Tomas said, "If you ever find a small brass key, don't give it to anybody. I'll explain everything when I can." He hung up before she could ask any more questions.

At ten o'clock, a tall woman in a green coat walked in. She said she was Mrs Carter, the mayor. "The clock on the town hall has been broken for years," she explained. "Your uncle always said he would fix it, but he never did. If you repair it, the town will be very grateful."
Elena felt nervous, but she agreed. "I'll go and have a look this afternoon," she said.

The tower was cold and dark. Elena climbed up the narrow stairs with her tools and found the old machine behind a wooden door. It was covered in dust. She cleaned it carefully, and after two hours she found something strange. Behind one of the big wheels there was a small metal box, tied to the frame with wire.
She opened it. Inside was a brass key with a number on it: 14. Her heart was beating fast. She remembered her uncle's words and put the key in her pocket.
When she went down, she saw a man in a long coat near the door. He was looking at her hands. "Did you find anything up there?" he asked in a friendly voice.
"Only a lot of dust," said Elena. "Who are you?"

parts.intro: Elena follows the clue and learns a secret from the past.
paragraphs: That evening, Elena sat in the shop and looked at the key. Where could number 14 be? She called Mr Hale and asked him if he had any idea.
"A key with a number? Hmm," he said, scratching his head. "The old railway station has a left-luggage room with lockers. It closed years ago, but nobody has ever taken the lockers away."

The next morning, she went to the station. The building was empty and the paint was coming off the walls. In the back room she found a row of old metal lockers. Number 14 was at the bottom. The key turned easily, and the door opened with a loud noise.
Inside there was a thick brown envelope. Elena sat on the floor and read the papers. There were old letters, bank records and a notebook written in her uncle's handwriting.

Slowly, she understood. Twenty years earlier, the town had collected money to build a new school. Mr Grant's father, who worked for the council, had said that the money was safe. But the records showed that he had taken most of it. Her uncle had found the proof by accident when he had been repairing the town clock. The council had hidden the papers inside it.
At the end of the notebook, Tomas had written: "I was afraid to tell the truth, because Grant's family was powerful. I hope someone braver than me will do it one day."
Elena's hands were shaking. As a bank worker, she knew very well what the numbers meant. She took photographs of every page with her phone. Then she heard footsteps behind her.
"I knew you would come here," said Mr Grant from the door. He was no longer smiling. "Give me the envelope, and I'll pay you a lot of money."

parts.intro: The truth comes out, and Elena decides what to do with her new life.
paragraphs: The police took Mr Grant away, and Elena gave the envelope and her photographs to the officer. That afternoon, she went to the town hall and told Mrs Carter everything. The mayor listened without saying a word. When Elena finished, she took off her glasses and sighed.
"My grandfather lost his savings in that school project," she said quietly. "For years, we thought it was just bad luck."

The news travelled fast. In a few days, everybody in town was talking about it. The council promised to check all the old records, and a judge said that the Grant family would have to give back the money. Mr Grant told the police that he had been looking for the papers for months. His father had always warned him that someone might find them.
Elena called her uncle in Canada and told him the story. He was silent for a long time. "I should have been braver," he finally said. "You did what I couldn't do. Thank you."

The office was bright and noisy, and every screen showed the same graph: a line climbing steadily upwards. Veridan sold software that predicted what customers would buy next, and its predictions were so accurate that larger companies were queuing up to sign contracts.

"Don't be nervous," said Daniel Reyes, the senior engineer who had been assigned to show her around. He was tall, relaxed and always smiling. "By Friday you'll feel as if you've worked here for years."

Nina wasn't so sure. She had left a secure job at a bank to join Veridan, and her parents had thought she was making a terrible mistake. If the company failed, she would have no safety net. Even so, she couldn't help feeling that something extraordinary was happening here.
The tour went smoothly until they reached the third floor. At the end of a quiet corridor stood a heavy grey door with a keypad. A low, steady hum was coming from behind it.
"What's in there?" Nina asked.

Daniel's smile didn't change, but he answered a little too quickly. "Just the main servers. Only Elena has access. She's the founder, and she's very protective of the code. You know what founders are like."
"Surely the servers would be in the basement," Nina said. "Or in a data centre somewhere."
"Most people would say so." He shrugged and moved on. "Come on, I'll show you the kitchen. The coffee is the best thing about this place."

That afternoon, Nina met Elena Vargas herself. The founder was a small woman in her fifties with sharp eyes and a very quiet voice. She shook Nina's hand and held it for a moment longer than necessary.
"I read your application three times," Elena said. "You must be extremely careful with data. That's rare, and I need it."
"I try to be," Nina replied. "At my last job, one wrong number could cost a customer a lot of money."
"Good. Because here, nothing is as simple as it looks." Elena looked at her for a long second. "Whatever you do, never ask me about the third floor. Not yet."

Nina nodded, but the warning only made her curious. All week she found herself walking past the grey door. Each time, the hum seemed to be slightly louder, almost as if the machine behind it were alive and waiting.

parts.intro: Nina notices a strange record in the system and begins to doubt the people around her.
paragraphs: On Monday morning, Nina could not stop thinking about the light under the door. She told herself that there was probably a simple explanation: the cleaners might have used a different entrance, or Elena might have arrived before sunrise. Nevertheless, a small voice in her head kept asking questions.

At ten o'clock she began a routine check of the company's access logs. It was a boring task, and she had expected nothing unusual. Then she saw it. At 3:12 a.m. on Saturday, someone had logged in with her username and copied an enormous file to an outside address.
Nina stared at the screen. She hadn't been near the building on Saturday. She had been at her cousin's wedding, dancing and eating cake until after midnight. The login couldn't have been hers.

Her hands began to shake. If she had reported the strange login immediately, the company might have stopped the copy in time, but she had only found it two days later. Now the file was gone, and her name was attached to the crime.

She considered going straight to Elena. Then she hesitated. Who could have known her password? She had only written it down once, on a note that she'd given to Daniel on her first day so that he could set up her laptop. He had promised to throw it away.
"You look terrible," Daniel said at lunch, putting a tray down beside her. "Did you sleep badly?"
"I'm fine," Nina lied. She didn't want to accuse anyone without proof. "It's just a lot of new information."

"You're doing great, you know." He lowered his voice. "Between you and me, Elena has been very strange lately. She spends whole nights on that third floor. If I were you, I wouldn't trust her too much."

The comment surprised Nina. Only an hour earlier, Daniel had spoken about Elena with great respect. Either he had changed his opinion very suddenly, or he was trying to push her in a particular direction.

That evening she changed her password and added a second security step to her account. Then she did something far more risky. She copied the suspicious log entry onto a small memory stick and put it in her pocket.

By Wednesday, she had made up her mind. The only way to learn the truth was to see inside the locked room. She knew that the keypad accepted a code, and she had noticed that Elena always typed it with her left hand, very fast, on the left side of the pad. Nina could not read the numbers, but she could see which keys had become worn and shiny.
Only four keys showed any wear. The code was a combination of those four numbers, repeated or reordered. It would take time, but it was possible.
At nine that night, when the building was silent again, she walked quietly towards the grey door.

parts.title: Part 3: What the Servers Were Hiding
parts.intro: Nina finally enters the forbidden room and finds an answer that raises even bigger questions.
paragraphs: It took Nina forty minutes to find the right code. When the lock finally clicked, she held her breath and pushed the heavy door open.

She had expected rows of machines and blinking lights. Instead, the room was small and surprisingly cold. A single computer glowed on a desk in the corner. The humming noise was coming from a large cooling unit fixed to the wall. Everything else was almost empty.
"This can't be the main server," she whispered. "It's far too small."

She sat down and woke the screen. The computer wasn't protected by a password, which struck her as bizarre in such a secretive company. A folder was open, and its name made her heart sink: Brightwell Archive.

Brightwell was a rival firm that had gone out of business two years earlier. Its customer data had never been made public, and everyone had assumed it had been destroyed. Yet here were thousands of records, with dates, names and purchase histories. The huge file that had been copied on Saturday was sitting in the folder as well.

Nina felt sick. So Veridan's famous accuracy was based on stolen information. No wonder the predictions had been so remarkable. The company must have used the Brightwell data to train its software from the very beginning.
"I told you not to ask about this room."
Nina spun round. Elena Vargas was standing in the doorway, wearing a coat over her pyjamas, with a mug in her hand. She looked exhausted rather than angry.
"It was you," Nina said, standing up. "You stole their data. And you used my account to copy it so that I would take the blame."
"That's what you think happened?" Elena asked calmly.
"What else could have happened? Nobody else has the key code."

"A great deal could have happened." Elena closed the door behind her. "If I had wanted to hide this, I would have changed the code months ago. Did you never wonder why I kept the same one for so long?"
Nina hesitated. It was true that the worn keys had made the code easy to guess. Almost as if it had been left like that on purpose.
"Sit down," Elena said. "You have two choices. You can call the police now, and Veridan will be finished by tomorrow. Or you can listen to me for ten minutes. Then you can decide."
Nina looked at the screen, then at the tired woman in front of her. Her instincts told her to run. But her curiosity, as usual, was stronger.
"Ten minutes," she said. "Start talking."

parts.title: Part 4: The Trap
parts.intro: Elena finally explains the truth, and Nina learns who she can really trust.
paragraphs: Elena sat on the edge of the desk and rubbed her eyes. "The data is real," she said. "But I didn't steal it. Brightwell's owner sold me its archive legally, years ago, when the company closed. I should have told our clients, and I didn't. That was my mistake, and I will answer for it."
"Then why is it hidden?" Nina asked.

"Because someone has been trying to blackmail me. Six months ago, a message arrived demanding money. If I hadn't paid, they said, they would tell everyone that I had used Brightwell's records. I paid once. Then I started to look for the person responsible."
Nina frowned. "You think it's someone inside Veridan."

"I know it is. Only a few people could have found this room. So I set a trap. I kept the same code, I left the computer unlocked, and I waited for someone to copy the file. I also made sure the thief would believe your account was the easiest to use."
"You used me as bait?" Nina said, furious.

"I did. And I'm sorry. But I needed somebody new, somebody who hadn't been involved in anything yet." Elena took a small tablet from her pocket. "The thief didn't know that this room records every visitor with a camera. Look."

On the screen, a grainy video showed a figure entering the room at 3:10 a.m. on Saturday. The man sat at the computer, copied the file and left. When he turned his face towards the camera, Nina's stomach turned over.
It was Daniel.
"He told me not to trust you," Nina said slowly. "He wanted me to believe you were the villain. He must have planned to leave my name on the logs and disappear."
"He was selling the data to a competitor," Elena said. "The blackmail was his idea too. He could easily have taken the money and left, but greed made him careless."

The next morning, the police were waiting in the lobby when Daniel arrived. He didn't even try to run. He simply looked at Nina and said, "I'd never have used your password if I'd thought you were clever enough to catch me." Nina almost laughed. It was the nicest compliment he had ever given her, and also the last.

Veridan survived, although not without difficulty. Elena informed every client about the archive, paid a large fine and accepted strict new rules about her data. As for Nina, she was promoted within the year. Her parents finally stopped worrying, and she still has a habit that colleagues find strange: she never writes down a password, and she always notices which keys on a keypad are wearing out.

parts.title: Part 1: The comfort of putting things off
parts.intro: The article argues that procrastination is better understood as an emotional habit than as a failure of time management.
paragraphs: Few habits are as widely condemned, and as widely practised, as procrastination. Almost everyone has, at some point, watched a deadline approach while choosing to alphabetise a bookshelf instead. The conventional explanation is that procrastinators are simply lazy or poorly organised. Yet a growing body of psychological research suggests that this diagnosis misses the point entirely: it is not time that we are failing to manage, but emotion.

The argument runs as follows. When a task evokes anxiety, boredom or self-doubt, avoiding it brings immediate relief. That relief acts as a reward, and rewards, as behaviourists have long observed, strengthen whatever behaviour precedes them. Seldom does the procrastinator consciously decide to sabotage the project; rather, the mind quietly trades long-term interests for short-term comfort. Only later, when the deadline looms, does the cost become painfully apparent.

Central to this account is the notion of present bias, the tendency to overvalue rewards that are close at hand and to discount those that lie in the future. A reward arriving in six months feels abstract, whereas the pleasure of checking one's phone is available right now. Not only does the future self seem remote, but some studies suggest we may think of that person almost as a stranger, someone else who will inherit the workload. It is hardly surprising, then, that we are so generous in handing unpleasant tasks over to them.

What makes procrastination so persistent is that it feeds on itself. Having delayed a task, people typically feel guilty, and guilt is itself an unpleasant emotion that invites further avoidance. Perfectionism complicates matters still further. Those who set unreasonably high standards may postpone beginning precisely because the work, once started, will inevitably fall short of the vision in their heads. Few forms of delay are more ironic than putting off a project because one cares about it too much.

If the problem is emotional, the solutions ought to be as well. Time-management techniques, such as colour-coded calendars and elaborate to-do lists, can help, but they address the symptom rather than the cause. More promising, according to many researchers, is self-compassion. In one frequently cited line of experiments, students who forgave themselves for putting off revision were less likely to delay the next time round than those who berated themselves. Although such findings should be interpreted with caution, they suggest that harshness is not the motivator we assume it to be.

Practical strategies follow naturally from this view. Breaking a daunting project into absurdly small steps lowers the emotional threshold for starting, and committing to just five minutes of work often proves enough to generate momentum. Likewise, making the future reward more vivid, or the temptation less accessible, tilts the balance back in favour of the long term. A person who leaves the phone in another room has not become more disciplined, merely more strategic.

None of this is to say that all delay is harmful. Some creative thinkers argue that a period of apparent idleness allows ideas to mature, and that rushing to act can be just as costly as avoiding action altogether. The distinction lies in intention: deliberate postponement, chosen with open eyes, is a strategy, whereas habitual avoidance, driven by discomfort, is a trap. Learning to tell the two apart may be the most useful skill of all.
Ultimately, it is worth asking not why we are so undisciplined, but what we are trying to escape. Once that question has been answered honestly, the bookshelf can remain unsorted a little longer.

parts.title: Part 2: Why words slip away
parts.intro: The article explains why newly learned words are forgotten and how research suggests learners can make them last.
paragraphs: Anyone who has crammed vocabulary the night before a test knows the peculiar sensation of mastery that evaporates within days. The words felt solid at midnight; by the weekend, they have dissolved. This frustrating experience is not a personal failing but a well-documented feature of human memory, and understanding it has profound implications for how languages are best learned.

Over a century ago, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised lists of meaningless syllables and measured how quickly he forgot them. His findings, now known as the forgetting curve, showed that retention drops steeply soon after learning and then levels off. What matters is not merely that forgetting occurs, but that it follows a predictable pattern, one which can be worked with rather than against.

The most robust insight to emerge from subsequent research is the spacing effect. Reviewing material at gradually widening intervals produces far more durable memories than cramming the same amount of study into a single session. Each time we retrieve a half-forgotten word, the effort of doing so strengthens the memory trace. Paradoxically, it is the difficulty of recall, not its ease, that makes learning stick. Psychologists refer to this as a 'desirable difficulty'.

A related finding concerns testing. Rereading a text feels productive because the material seems familiar, yet familiarity is a poor guide to genuine knowledge. By contrast, closing the book and trying to recall what one has read, or to produce a sentence using a new word, exposes gaps and consolidates what is already known. Learners who test themselves regularly tend to outperform those who simply review, even though the latter often feel more confident.

Language learning adds further complications. A word is not an isolated fact but a node in a network of sounds, meanings, grammatical behaviours and associations. The richer the connections, the more routes there are back to the word when it is needed. This is why encountering vocabulary in varied contexts, rather than in tidy translated lists, appears to be so effective. Hearing 'tackle' in a sports commentary, a news story and a conversation about a difficult problem builds a flexible understanding that no single definition could provide.

Sleep, too, plays a part that is easily underestimated. Evidence from laboratory studies suggests that memories are reorganised during sleep, with newly acquired information being integrated into existing knowledge. A learner who studies in the evening and sleeps well may therefore retain more than one who stays up late revising. Admittedly, the precise mechanisms remain debated, and it would be unwise to claim that a good night's rest can substitute for practice.

Does this mean that technology can solve the problem? Flashcard applications that schedule reviews automatically have undoubtedly made spaced repetition accessible to millions. Nevertheless, a tool is only as useful as the habits surrounding it. Many learners accumulate thousands of cards yet never use the words in conversation, and a word that has never been spoken or written remains, in an important sense, borrowed rather than owned.

The lesson, then, is a modest one. Effective learning is rarely dramatic; it resembles gardening more than construction, rewarding steady attention over heroic effort. Forgetting is not the enemy of learning but a part of the process, a signal that a memory is ready to be strengthened. Those who accept this are likely to find that progress, though gradual, proves far more lasting than any last-minute sprint.

parts.title: Part 3: Streets for people, not only for cars
parts.intro: The article looks at how cities came to be built around cars and at the debate over making them friendlier to pedestrians.
paragraphs: Stand on almost any major street in the world and ask what it is for. In many cities, the honest answer would be: moving cars. Roads occupy a staggering share of urban land, parking lots swallow prime locations, and pedestrians are expected to wait patiently at crossings designed to keep traffic flowing. It was not always so. The dominance of the car in city planning is a relatively recent development, the product of choices made in the twentieth century rather than of any natural law.

Those choices were made with good intentions. Planners faced growing populations and the promise of personal mobility, and they responded by widening roads, building highways through established neighbourhoods and separating homes from workplaces and shops. Only decades later did the costs become evident. Traffic, far from disappearing, expanded to fill the space provided, a phenomenon often called induced demand. Build a wider road, and more people will drive, until congestion returns.

A different philosophy has gained ground in recent years. Rather than asking how to move vehicles more efficiently, its advocates ask how to make places that people want to spend time in. Central to this approach is the idea of the walkable neighbourhood, where daily needs such as groceries, schools and parks lie within a short stroll or cycle ride. Such an arrangement is sometimes described as the 'fifteen-minute city', although the term has proved surprisingly controversial.

The controversy deserves attention. Critics have suggested that the concept is a pretext for restricting freedom of movement. Proponents reply that nothing in it forbids driving; the aim is to make alternatives genuinely attractive, so that residents have a choice. It is worth noting that a good deal of the disagreement stems from differing assumptions about who bears the cost of change. Shopkeepers, for instance, frequently fear that removing parking will drive customers away.

Evidence on this point is mixed but intriguing. Several cities that have pedestrianised central streets report that local businesses did not suffer as predicted, partly because people on foot tend to visit more often, even if they spend less on each visit. Yet it would be naive to assume that results from one place can be transplanted to another. Climate, density, public transport and local culture all shape what works.

Beyond economics lie questions of health and community. Streets that feel safe invite children to play, older people to walk and neighbours to meet by chance. Researchers have long noted that such casual encounters, though seemingly trivial, help build the trust on which communities depend. Reducing noise and air pollution brings obvious benefits, too. Not every improvement requires grand investment: planting trees, widening pavements and slowing traffic can transform a street at relatively modest cost.

Fairness cannot be ignored either. Improvements to a neighbourhood often raise property prices, and residents who endured years of neglect may find themselves priced out just as conditions improve. Planners who wish to avoid this outcome must think about affordable housing alongside cycle lanes. Similarly, people with disabilities, or those who depend on cars because of where they must work, deserve solutions rather than slogans.

What emerges, then, is not a crusade against the car but a rebalancing. A city is ultimately a shared space, and the question of whom it is designed for is as much political as technical. Those who answer 'everyone' take on a more demanding task than those who simply optimise traffic, but the reward is a place worth living in.

parts.title: Part 4: Who owns a style?
parts.intro: The article weighs the legal, economic and philosophical arguments in the debate over AI-generated art.
paragraphs: When an image generated by software won a prize at an art competition a few years ago, the reaction was swift and divided. Some saw a milestone; others saw a betrayal. Since then, the debate over AI-generated art has only grown more heated, drawing in lawyers, technologists, galleries and, above all, the artists whose work made the technology possible. What makes the discussion so difficult is that it involves not one question but several, each pulling in a different direction.

The first concerns how these systems are built. Image generators learn by analysing vast collections of existing pictures, many of which were gathered from the internet without the creators' knowledge. Defenders argue that this resembles how human artists learn: by studying the works of others and absorbing their techniques. Critics counter that the comparison is misleading. A student cannot reproduce thousands of styles in seconds, nor can a student's output be used to undercut the very people whose work was studied.

The legal position is unsettled. Courts in several countries are considering whether training on copyrighted material constitutes fair use or infringement, and it is far from clear how they will rule. Even if the practice is eventually deemed lawful, however, legality and legitimacy are not the same thing. Many people feel that something can be permitted by law and still be unfair, particularly when the benefits flow mainly to companies rather than to creators.

A second question is economic. Illustrators, concept artists and designers report that commissions have dried up as clients turn to cheaper automated alternatives. Enthusiasts reply that every new technology, from photography to digital editing, provoked similar alarm, and that creative professions adapted. The analogy is instructive but imperfect: photography did not depend on the unpaid labour of the painters it threatened. Whether the scale and speed of this change permit the same adaptation remains uncertain.

The third question, and perhaps the most philosophical, is whether the output counts as art at all. Some hold that art requires intention and lived experience, qualities a statistical model cannot possess. Others argue that meaning arises in the encounter between work and viewer, regardless of how the work was made. Neither position is easily dismissed. It may be more productive to recognise that people use the word 'art' to mean different things: craft, self-expression, commodity or conversation.

Practical proposals are beginning to emerge. Some advocate consent-based systems, in which artists can opt in or out of training datasets, perhaps with compensation. Others favour clear labelling, so that audiences know how an image was produced and can decide how to value it. Neither measure would settle the deeper disagreements, but both would at least replace secrecy with transparency, which is a precondition for any serious debate.

It is also worth remembering that many artists are experimenting with the tools rather than rejecting them. For these practitioners, the software is another instrument, capable of producing the banal or the striking depending on the judgement of the person using it. This suggests that the technology's significance may depend less on what it can do than on who is allowed to shape its use.

No tidy conclusion is available. What seems certain is that the decisions made now, about consent, credit and compensation, will determine whether these tools enrich creative culture or hollow it out. Those decisions should not be left to engineers alone.

parts.title: Part 1: The Pane of Glass
parts.intro: A veteran translator receives a posthumous manuscript and boasts that she will remain invisible inside it.
paragraphs: I have always held that a good translator is a pane of glass: clean, unremarked, and, if the work is done properly, forgotten the moment anyone looks through it. It is a creed I recommend to the young, partly because it is true and partly because it keeps them quiet.

The manuscript arrived on a Tuesday in November, in a box that had clearly been sealed by someone who distrusted tape. Inside lay four hundred and twelve typed pages, a note from the publisher in the clipped dialect of people who pay late, and nothing else. No photograph of the author, no biography, not even a pencilled apology for the state of the footnotes. The title page read The Salt Ledger, by one Anselm Voss, deceased, which I took to be a professional courtesy: the dead make the least troublesome clients.

I should say at the outset that I am not a woman given to fancy. My flat is on the fourth floor of a building whose lift has been out of order since the previous administration, and I climb the stairs each evening with the grim satisfaction of someone who has never once asked for help. My sister says this is a character flaw. I say it is a pension plan.

For the first sixty pages the book behaved itself. It concerned a harbour town, a family of ropemakers, and a quarrel over an inheritance, all rendered in the long, rolling sentences that Voss's language permits and mine merely tolerates. I worked from nine until one, then from three until seven, with the discipline of a monk who has been told the monastery is being sold. I ate standing up. I translated 'the sea declined to forgive them' three different ways before settling on the plainest, which is, I have found, usually the one that wounds.

It was on page sixty-one that the heroine, a woman named Ilka, sat down at her kitchen table and stirred three sugars into a cup of tea she did not intend to drink. 'It was a habit,' wrote Voss, 'that she had inherited from her mother along with the chipped blue cup, and she would have denied it under oath.'

I put down my pencil. This was not, I wish to be clear, the response of a woman given to fancy. It was the response of a woman who had, that very morning, stirred three sugars into a cup of tea she did not intend to drink, using a chipped blue cup that had belonged to her mother, and who would have denied it under oath.

Naturally, I laughed. Three sugars is hardly a fingerprint. Half the continent sweetens its grief. As for the cup, chipped blue crockery is the common currency of dead mothers; one could furnish a small museum with it. I made a fresh pot, drank it black and in protest, and returned to the page with the faintly theatrical briskness of someone resolved to notice nothing.

But a translator is, by trade, a person who notices everything and then says it in another language. That is the whole difficulty of the profession. By evening I had found Ilka's habit of counting the stairs aloud when she was frightened, which I do, and her distaste for the colour yellow, which I share, and a limp, the legacy of an old fall from a bicycle, that Voss placed in the left ankle, which is precisely where mine lives.

I closed the manuscript at seven exactly, as a matter of principle. Then I stood at the window for some time, watching the streetlamps come on in their orderly sequence, like an argument being made by someone who has already won it.
'Coincidence,' I said aloud to the empty room, and the room, being a good listener, did not contradict me.

parts.title: Part 2: A Hardy Plant
parts.intro: The coincidences refuse to stay coincidences, and a phone call with her sister unsettles the narrator's memory.
paragraphs: Coincidence, I discovered, is a hardy plant: it will grow in almost any soil, provided one waters it daily with denial. I watered mine assiduously for a week.

By the second week, however, the book had stopped pretending. In chapter nine, Ilka received a letter from a man she had once refused to marry, and she read it standing in the hallway with her coat still on, then filed it, unanswered, between the pages of a cookery book. I have such a letter. I have such a cookery book. I did not, I assured myself, need to check the shelf, and so I checked the shelf, and there it was, the spine cracked at exactly the chapter on preserves, the envelope still furred with a decade's dust.
I rang my sister that evening. Perpetua and I speak on Sundays by custom and on other days by catastrophe, and she answered on the second ring, which told me she had already assumed the latter.
'Nothing is wrong,' I said. 'I am merely conducting a small survey. Do you remember whether I ever told you about Tomas's letter?'
'Which Tomas?'
'Precisely.' I was pleased with this; it was the answer of a witness who has not been coached. 'And the cup. The blue one. Do you remember who had it last?'
'You did,' said Perpetua. 'You took it from the house the week we cleared it. You said it would be wasteful to throw away a perfectly good cup, and then you cried in the car for forty minutes.'
'I did nothing of the kind.'
'Helena, I was driving.'

I let that pass, as one lets pass a bus that is going in the wrong direction. It was, after all, my sister's version of events, and my sister has always had a weakness for the dramatic; as a child she insisted that the wardrobe contained a bishop. I thanked her, promised to call on Sunday, and hung up with the cool dignity of a woman who has not been contradicted by anyone of consequence.
Then I sat for a long while with the receiver in my lap, listening to the flat, patient hum of the dial tone as if it were a verdict.

The difficulty, you understand, was not that Voss knew things. A novelist is a kind of burglar; he enters the house of the human heart through the window and takes whatever he finds. The difficulty was that Voss knew them in my order. Ilka's secrets emerged in the same sequence in which I had arranged my own, the small shames first, set out like the good china, the large ones kept in the cellar for as long as the furniture would allow. No stranger shuffles another person's guilt so exactly. It was the work of someone who had sat in the next room for forty years with a glass pressed to the wall.

I made enquiries, naturally, with the thoroughness of a woman who prefers facts to feelings, mostly because facts do not ask how you are. The publisher's assistant, a pleasant young man who pronounced my name as though it were a diagnosis, told me that Anselm Voss had died in a hospice by the coast, that he had left no family, and that the manuscript had been found in a drawer 'with a note addressed to the translator.'
'Which translator?' I asked.
'Well,' he said, and I heard him turn a page, 'it says "to whoever is sensible enough to be afraid of it". We assumed that was a joke.'
'Naturally,' I said. 'A joke.'

I did not sleep that night, which I put down to the tea. I had, of course, resumed drinking it with sugar. There seemed little point in resisting any longer, and it is a curious comfort, when one is being written, to be at least a consistent character.

parts.title: Part 3: Eleven Visits
parts.intro: A chapter threatens to expose a fact the narrator has hidden for years, and she tests the limits of her professional rule.
paragraphs: There is a rule in my profession, rarely spoken aloud because it flatters no one: the translator may smooth, may soften, may even, in extremity, omit; but she may not lie. I had lived by it for thirty years, and it had never once been tested, for the simple reason that nobody had ever written down anything I wished to keep hidden.
Chapter fourteen tested it in the first paragraph.

Ilka's mother, in the book, grew old in a house by the water and was moved, in the autumn of her eighty-first year, to a care home forty miles inland. Ilka signed the papers on a Thursday. She chose the home, Voss tells us, for its gravel drive, its fresh paint, and its distance, and she told everyone that the distance was a matter of the garden. She visited eleven times in two years. Voss does not comment on the number; he merely lists the dates, with the unblinking courtesy of a clerk reading out a will.

I know the number. I have never told it to anyone, not to Perpetua, not to the priest whom I stopped visiting, and not, for most of the last decade, to myself. It lives in the cellar with the good wine and the bad news.

I did what any person of principle would do: I made tea, and I made a plan. The plan was elegant, and it had the great advantage of being entirely professional. Voss's syntax at this point grows tangled; a certain looseness in the tenses leaves it unclear whether Ilka visited eleven times or merely intended to. A translator is permitted, indeed obliged, to resolve ambiguity, and I resolved it in the kindest direction. Ilka visited often. Ilka visited, in my English, so frequently that the nurses knew her by name.

I read the sentence back and found it excellent. It had a warmth I should have been proud of in any other circumstances. Then I read the original again, and the original, which was not warm in the least, looked back at me with an expression I can only describe as patience.

It is a remarkable thing to be corrected by a dead man. I had always imagined that the dead, if they spoke, would raise their voices. Voss did nothing of the kind. He had simply set down the truth in a clean, rather beautiful sentence, and left it lying on the page like a coin on a counter, certain that I would eventually pick it up.

I should record, in fairness to myself, that I resisted for three days. I took long walks. I cleaned the oven, a task I had not undertaken since the Berlin Wall came down. I wrote to the publisher proposing that the chapter be cut on grounds of pace, and received a reply so courteous that it could only have been written by someone who had not read it. On the fourth morning I climbed the four flights with a bag of shopping, felt the old ankle protest as it always does, and counted the steps aloud in the stairwell, quietly, as I have done since childhood, and understood that I had been counting them for the whole of this book.

That afternoon I translated the chapter as it stood. Eleven visits. Eleven, in plain English, with no adverbs to cushion the fall. My hands, I noticed, were perfectly steady, and that frightened me more than a tremor would have done, because a steady hand is only a sign that the heart has stopped arguing.

When I had finished, I did something I have not done since I was a girl. I went to the window, opened it, and said the number into the evening air, once, aloud, to see whether the street would object. The street did not. A man walked a dog. A bus sighed at the corner. The world, as ever, was too busy to forgive me, and for that small mercy I was almost grateful.

parts.title: Part 4: The Missing Verb
parts.intro: The final pages arrive, and the narrator must choose how a sentence, and perhaps a life, will end.
paragraphs: The last chapter reached me on the twenty-third of December, which is to say that I reached it, having approached it for weeks in the manner of a swimmer testing cold water with one toe. It was only four pages long. Voss, who had never hurried anything, seemed to have lost patience with himself in the closing stretch, and the sentences came shorter, plainer, stripped of their ropes and rigging, like a ship that has decided to stop pretending it is going anywhere but home.

I have withheld one fact until now, and you will forgive me; a translator, like a good host, saves the cheese for the end. In the final chapter we learn that Ilka, the ropemaker's daughter, has spent her life translating other people's books. She sits at her kitchen table with a stranger's manuscript, a cup of sweet tea going cold at her elbow, and discovers that the pages describe her. She laughs. She tells herself it is coincidence. She is, Voss writes, 'a woman not given to fancy.'
I read that line eleven times, which seemed fitting.

There was a second discovery, smaller and in some ways worse. I had spent a month admiring Voss's typescript for its clean, old-fashioned look, and only now, in the clear light of a winter morning, did I notice that the lowercase e sinks slightly below the line, a defect that no one would choose and that I would know anywhere. I owned a typewriter with that flaw. I sold it in 1994 to a man who did not give his name and paid, I recall, in coins.
I do not draw conclusions from this. I am a translator, not a detective, and the profession teaches one to distrust anyone who is too sure of what a sentence means.

The book ends in mid-air. Ilka types the final full stop, rises from the table, takes her coat from its hook, and the last line of the manuscript reads, in the original, 'Then Ilka put on her coat and' and there it stops, without a verb, without a full stop, hanging over the white margin like a foot over a stair. Beneath it, in pencil, in a hand that trembles but is not unkind, are three words: 'Yours to finish.'

For a day I did nothing. I let the line sit in the flat like a guest who has not been asked to leave. I thought of the tea, and the cup, and the eleven dates, and the long gravel drive that I have, in the privacy of my own cellar, driven up in my head a great many times without ever once reaching the door. I considered the verbs available to me. A weaker woman would have chosen 'wept', a vainer one 'wrote', and a woman wishing to be admired by the critics would have chosen something with a great deal of weather in it.

On Christmas Eve, at about four in the afternoon, I typed one word, on a modern machine with a perfectly behaved e, and closed the file. I will not tell you which word it was. A translator, like a confessor, is trusted precisely because she is not heard. The publisher may print the book as it stands; the critics may admire or ignore it; the verb, I suspect, will matter only to two people, one of whom is dead.

But I will tell you what happened afterwards, since it is a matter of record. I took the cup down from the shelf, washed it, and placed it, with a certain ceremony, in the cardboard box I had set aside for the post. I looked up the timetable for the inland train. It leaves at ten. I have bought a ticket, as a matter of research, and my coat is on the chair.
Then I went out to the stairs, and, from habit, began to count them aloud. There are sixty-one. I had never known.
